sections.html:
Washington County sits in eastern Nebraska just north of Douglas County and the Omaha area, with Blair as the county seat. The 2020 count was 20,865 people. Most of the land is farmland, with Blair and Fort Calhoun as the cities and Arlington, Herman, Kennard and Washington as villages.

A homeowner here may live in a town, in a village or on a rural parcel, and that choice decides which municipal rules apply on top of the county's. Low ground near the Missouri River carries flood risk, as the 2011 river floods near the Blair bridge showed.

Four offices matter to a property owner, and each has a separate job.

OfficeWhat it doesHow to reach it
County AssessorSets valuations and reviews them before a protestCall the Assessor's office
County ClerkReceives Form 422 protests for the Board of Equalization1555 Colfax Street, Blair, NE 68008; (402) 426-6822; mail to P.O. Box 466
County TreasurerCollects real and personal property taxP.O. Box 348, Blair, NE 68008; (402) 426-6888
Register of DeedsRecords deeds and collects deed taxCall the Register of Deeds

sections.h2: How Nebraska values a home here
sections.html:
Property is assessed as of January 1 each year. Houses, rural homes, buildings, commercial and industrial property, recreational property and mobile homes are held to 100 percent of market value. Agricultural land is held to 75 percent of market value and is valued from soil maps and land use such as dry, irrigated or grassland.

Your tax is the taxable value multiplied by the consolidated rate for your tax district, stated per $100 of value. A house inside a town pays county, municipal and school district levies together, so two houses with the same value can get different bills if they sit in different districts.

The assessor sends a notice by June 1 to the owner of record as of May 20 for any parcel whose value changed. Homestead exemption applications can exempt all or part of a home's value for qualifying owners, and they are filed with the assessor between February 1 and June 30.

File Form 422 with the County Clerk on or before June 30. Talk to the Assessor's staff first, because that conversation may make a protest unnecessary.

  1. Ask the Assessor's office how the value was set.
  2. File Form 422 with the Clerk by June 30, stating the value you request, the basis for it and the legal description. A protest without reasons can be dismissed.
  3. Ask for a review by the Assessor's office if you want one. A referee who is a registered appraiser may meet with you before the Board of Equalization hearing.
  4. Attend the hearing. The Clerk tells you the time and place and notifies you of the Board's decision within seven days of the final action.
  5. If you disagree, appeal to the Tax Equalization and Review Commission within 30 days after the Board adjourns. For protests handled in the June 1 to July 25 session, adjournment is deemed July 25.

A protest covers valuation only. It is not a challenge to the tax rate. Comparable sales or a recent appraisal are the usual evidence for a house. Personal property protests are due earlier, by May 1.

Real and personal property taxes are due December 31. The first half becomes delinquent the following May 1 and the second half on September 1. Nebraska sets interest on delinquent taxes owed to political subdivisions at 14 percent a year. This calendar differs from Douglas County, so anyone who moved up from Omaha should reset their reminders.

Mail payments to the Washington County Treasurer, P.O. Box 348, Blair, NE 68008, or pay online through the county's payment vendor. On the due date, personal property tax becomes a first lien on all personal property you own, and that property can be seized to satisfy it.

Unpaid real estate tax can lead to a county tax sale. Nebraska Revised Statute 77-1801 ties the sale of delinquent real property to the first Monday of March, and Statute 77-1802 requires the county treasurer to prepare a list of delinquent real property four to six weeks before that Monday. If you own a house with back taxes, ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure early. It gives you the most choices, whether you pay, sell or negotiate a sale.

If taxes are owed at closing, they are normally paid from the sale proceeds through the title company, which also splits the current year's bill between buyer and seller. A house with delinquent taxes can still close, because the payoff usually comes out of the price.

  • Call the Treasurer at (402) 426-6888 for a balance before you sign anything.
  • Ask the title company for its settlement statement ahead of the signing date.
  • Confirm that no earlier year is still open.

The Register of Deeds records a sale. It charges $10 for the first page and $6 for each added page, with certified copies at $1.50 a page. A Real Estate Transfer Statement, Form 521, must accompany the deed.

The Nebraska documentary stamp tax is $3.32 for each $1,000 of value for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026, and it falls on the grantor. Rely on the state's current number when you budget for closing.

faqs.q: When is the Washington County, Nebraska property tax protest deadline?
faqs.a: Real property protests must be filed with the County Clerk on or before June 30. Personal property protests are due by May 1. Use Form 422, state the value you want and explain why.

faqs.q: When do Washington County taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: The first half is delinquent after May 1 and the second half after September 1, following the December 31 due date. Interest is 14 percent a year under Nebraska law. You can pay by mail to P.O. Box 348 in Blair or online.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house in Washington County if I owe property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Back taxes are normally paid from the proceeds at closing, and the title company confirms the payoff. Get a balance from the Treasurer, phone (402) 426-6888, before you sign anything.

faqs.q: Who do I call to dispute my Washington County property value?
faqs.a: Start with the County Assessor's office, then file Form 422 with the County Clerk at 1555 Colfax Street in Blair if the issue remains. The Clerk's number is (402) 426-6822.

faqs.q: How is farmland valued compared with a house?
faqs.a: Houses and other buildings are valued at 100 percent of market. Agricultural land is held to 75 percent of market and is valued from soil maps and land use.
